summary: Czechia is part of the EU and the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (the ETIAS travel authorization is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90.

TR.notes: A Schengen short-stay visa is required. Under the EU Visa Code, when Czechia is your only or main destination, you apply to the consulate of Czechia (or of the Schengen state representing it) competent for the place where you legally reside.

RU.notes: A Schengen short-stay visa is required, at the standard €90 fee. The Czech Foreign Ministry says Czechia restricts visa services for Russian citizens in response to the aggression against Ukraine, and since 3 July 2024 recognizes only biometric Russian passports (children under 15 excepted). The European Commission says that since 7 November 2025 Russian nationals no longer receive multiple-entry visas and must apply for a new visa for each trip, with exceptions for limited, justified cases such as independent journalists and human rights defenders.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: EUR-Lex — Regulation (EU) 2016/399 (Schengen Borders Code), consolidated text
source.instrument: Regulation (EU) 2016/399 (Schengen Borders Code), Art. 6(1) (90 days in any 180-day period) and Art. 6(2) (the date of entry is the first day of stay and the date of exit the last)

proofOfFunds.text: Non-EU visitors must possess sufficient funds for their stay. The Foreign Ministry sets the amount from the Czech existential minimum: at least CZK 1,565 per day for stays of up to 30 days, and CZK 46,950 plus CZK 6,260 for each full month for longer stays. A bank statement with an internationally accepted bank card, a prepaid voucher or an officially verified invitation can serve as proof.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border on your first crossing since the EES started; the EU says it can be quicker if you register some of your data in advance. The UK government's travel advice says there is no cost for EES registration.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

source.name: Your Europe (EU) — travelling with cash

notes: Entering from outside the EU, the duty-free allowance is 200 cigarettes (or 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco), 1 litre of spirits over 22% (or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine), 4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, and other goods worth up to €300 (€430 by air or sea), according to the EU’s Your Europe portal.

The EU's Your Europe portal says that when you arrive from another EU country you pay no duty on alcohol and tobacco bought for your own use, and that above guideline values (such as 800 cigarettes or 10 litres of spirits) customs may ask you to prove they are for your own use.

payments.text: No official source we read describes card acceptance in Czechia. Czechia does not use the euro; the currency is the Czech koruna (CZK). The Government of Canada says non-official currency exchange is illegal and advises using only official exchange offices or banks.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office says petty theft is a problem, especially in major tourist areas in Prague, and passes on Prague city police advice to change money only at an exchange office or bank because money changed on the street is often counterfeit. Canada's travel advice says violent crime is low and petty crime such as pickpocketing is common.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Czech Republic travel advice: safety and security

roadVignette.text: Czech motorways use an electronic vignette checked against the vehicle's licence plate. Low-emission vehicles pay a reduced eco price (70–150 CZK for 10 days, 640–1,280 CZK for a year, depending on the fuel system). The Police and the Customs Administration check plates with camera-equipped patrol cars on the toll road, at control gates and at rest stops and parking lots.

driving.text: Czechia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Czechia yet.

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Czechia — days spent in Germany or Austria count against the same allowance.

Change money only at official exchange offices or banks. The Government of Canada says non-official currency exchange is illegal, and the UK FCDO reports Prague city police advice that money changed on the street is often counterfeit.

The Government of Canada and the UK FCDO advise against hailing taxis on the street in Prague. Canada advises using only officially marked taxis, reputable taxi companies or a trusted ride-sharing app, and the FCDO says to check the rates on the side of the taxi before getting in.

On your first crossing of a Schengen external border since the EES started, your fingerprints and photo are recorded at passport control. The EU says the process can be quicker if you register some of your data in advance.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Czechia?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Czechia and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Czech Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries, and applications are decided within 15–45 calendar days.

faq.question: Does Czechia use the euro?
faq.answer: No. Czechia uses the Czech koruna (CZK). The Government of Canada says non-official currency exchange is illegal: change money only at official exchange offices or banks, never with vendors on the street.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Czechia?
faq.answer: ETIAS for visa-exempt travelers is not yet in operation, and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. Once it starts, the application fee is EUR 20.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Czechia without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area. EU and EFTA citizens need no visa.
